<description>
Two test cases (`p2p_v2_encrypted.py` and `p2p_v2_misbehaving.py`) can fail in the -- improbable -- case when network reads happen to arrive in smaller chunks.

Related to #36726 .

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking. Normally, the chunking of the sends of the writer dictate the chunking of the receives at the reader, but this is not guaranteed by IP/TCP, intermediate networking elements may change the packet structure. In test using sockets on the same host, this is not very likely, but still possible.

Issues:

- `p2p_v2_encrypted.py`:  The v1 message parser in `P2PConnection` rejected the stream as soon as the first 4 bytes did not match the network magic. bitcoind's `V1Transport::readHeader` waits for the full 24-byte header before checking the magic.
The v2 to v1 downgrade relies on bitcoind's behaviour: an outbound v2 connection is only retried with v1 (`V2Transport::ShouldReconnectV1`) if at least a v1 header's worth of bytes had been sent before the peer disconnected. If the node's first send reaches the test peer in small pieces, the Python peer could disconnect after just 4 bytes, the node would not retry with v1, and p2p_v2_encrypted.py would time out waiting for the reconnection.

-  `p2p_v2_misbehaving.py`: Fails for similar root cause. In this test, when the 64-byte key could not be read in one call, the empty array is indexed out-of-bounds, leading to a crash.

The issues were found -- and can be reproduced -- by using a reproducer patch, that forces all socket sends to use smaller chunking. For the run with the reproducer see #36724 .

The issues are test-code only, the non-test code is correct.

The fixes are:

- `p2p_v2_encrypted.py`: Match bitcoind by checking the magic only once the full header has been received.

-  `p2p_v2_misbehaving.py`: Handle the short-read case explicitly, return the data read so far.

These fixes make the test more robust, even though a failure due to this issue in CI is very unlikely, but not impossible.
</description>

<commits>
be35cbb0b1 test: p2p: check v1 magic bytes only after the full header

The v1 message parser in P2PConnection rejected the stream as soon as
the first 4 bytes did not match the network magic. bitcoind's
V1Transport::readHeader waits for the full 24-byte header before
checking the magic.

The v2 to v1 downgrade relies on bitcoind's behaviour: an outbound v2
connection is only retried with v1 (V2Transport::ShouldReconnectV1)
if at least a v1 header's worth of bytes had been sent before the
peer disconnected. If the node's first send reaches the test peer in
small pieces, the Python peer could disconnect after just 4 bytes, the
node would not retry with v1, and p2p_v2_encrypted.py would time out
waiting for the reconnection.

Match bitcoind by checking the magic only once the full header has
been received.

be788a9ce4 test: p2p: Don't use empty garbage as "not yet responded" in v2 responder

When P2PConnection is the v2 responder, _on_data_v2_handshake() used
`not self.v2_state.sent_garbage` to decide whether it still had to send
its ellswift key. The garbage length is random in [0, MAX_GARBAGE_LEN],
so in about 1 in 4096 connections it is empty and the check stays true
after the key has been sent.

If the peer's 64-byte key then arrives in more than one piece,
complete_handshake() asks for more data, and on the next read the
responder runs respond_v2_handshake() again: it generates and sends a
second key, and misaligns the received key bytes. Both sides then wait
for a garbage terminator that never comes. With the test default
peertimeout=999999999 nobody times out, and the test can hang until its
own timeout.

Check whether our ellswift key has been generated instead.

baafaf8526 test: p2p_v2_misbehaving: Handle partial ellswift read

The node's 64-byte ellswift key can arrive in several chunks. In that
case EncryptedP2PState.complete_handshake() returns (0, b"") to signal
that more data is needed. The WrongGarbageTerminatorState override
bit-flipped the returned bytes unconditionally, which crashed in
random_bitflip() on empty input and dropped the connection.

Return the "need more data" result unchanged before tampering with it.

ba7dde0b75 test: v2_p2p: Return bytes consumed per call in respond_v2_handshake

respond_v2_handshake() returned len(self.received_prefix) as the number
of bytes consumed, and the caller trims recvbuf by that amount. But
received_prefix accumulates across calls, so when the v1 prefix check
spans more than one read, too many bytes are dropped from recvbuf.

This happens when the peer's ellswift key starts with bytes that match
the v1 prefix (e.g. the first network magic byte, about 1 in 256 keys)
and a read ends inside that matching part. The remaining key bytes are
then misaligned, the shared secret is wrong, and the handshake stalls.

Return only the number of bytes consumed in the current call.
</commits>
